sections.h2: Who collects property tax in Medina County
sections.html:
The Medina County Treasurer collects the bill. The office is in the County Administration Building at 144 North Broadway in Medina, and the phone number is 330-725-9748. The counter is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, and stays open until 6:00 p.m. on a due date.

Two offices split the work. The auditor values the parcels and handles exemptions. The treasurer sends the bills and takes the payments. The treasurer's website, which is separate from the auditor's, is where you look up a bill and pay it.

Bills come out twice a year. If yours never shows up, call the office or use the Search and Pay Taxes link on the treasurer's site. It lets you print an official bill to pay by mail or at the counter, so a missing bill is never a reason to miss the date.

Medina County sits in northeast Ohio, south and west of Cleveland. The 2020 census counted 182,470 residents, up from 172,332 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 185,025. Growth like that keeps demand for homes steady.

  • Value of an owned home at the midpoint: $287,000
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 80.3 percent
  • Household income at the midpoint: $94,968
  • Monthly cost for owners with a mortgage: $1,726
  • Gross rent at the midpoint: $1,143
  • Permits for new housing in 2025: 430

Those figures put Medina County at the high end of Ohio's county markets. Most sales here are owner to owner.

Ohio bills property tax in two halves. The 2026 first half came due February 27 and the second half August 28. Both dates ran later than in earlier years, when deadlines fell in early or mid February and in July. The second-half bills were late because the county auditor had to reprogram software for a new state law, and every one of Ohio's 88 counties had delays. The treasurer announces future dates each time bills go out, so look for the current notice instead of assuming last year's calendar.

Medina County 2026 installments
InstallmentBills and amountDue date and penalties
First half, tax year 202578,728 bills mailed, $412,675,472 billed for the full yearDue February 27, 2026. A 5 percent penalty if postmarked after that date and 10 percent after March 9
Second half, tax year 202567,566 bills mailed August 6, $204,658,816 billedDue August 28, 2026. A 5 percent penalty after that date and 10 percent after September 7

The year in the left column is the tax year, and it trails the calendar year in Ohio. A bill you pay in 2026 covers 2025.

sections.h2: How to pay a Medina County tax bill
sections.html:
The treasurer offers several routes. The vendor fees go to the vendors, not to the county.

  • Online. E-check costs $1.50. Debit cards carry a 1.99 percent fee, and credit cards or a PayPal account carry 2.5 percent.
  • Phone. Call 1-888-607-8389 to pay by e-check or card, with the same fees.
  • Counter. Bring the whole bill to 144 North Broadway. Checks, cash and credit cards are accepted.
  • Drop boxes. Twenty-four hour boxes stand at the Treasurer's office, Brunswick City Hall on Center Road, the Lodi Library on Wooster Street and the Wadsworth Municipal Building on Maple Street. Include the bill stub with a check.
  • PayPal Credit. The bill-me-later option spreads payment over six months with no interest, subject to credit approval and a 2.5 percent vendor charge. Some taxpayers use it to meet the due date and avoid the 10 percent penalty.

Mail is riskier than it used to be. Since December 2025 the postal service has postmarked mail at regional facilities, so a postmark may not match the day you dropped the envelope in a box. The treasurer goes by the postmark. Mail early, or ask a post office counter to hand-stamp the envelope.

sections.h2: What is the inflation cap credit?
sections.html:
House Bill 186 created a credit that limits increases on certain unvoted school taxes to the rate of inflation. Six of Medina County's eight school districts fell under the state's 20 mill floor: Black River, Brunswick, Buckeye, Cloverleaf, Highland and the Career Center. After the auditor's 2025 reappraisal raised values, those districts received more than $14 million in additional unvoted revenue. The cap sends about $5.5 million back to taxpayers, and it appears on the second-half bill as Inflation Cap Credit.

Not every owner gets it, because only six of the eight districts were affected. If a second-half bill shows no credit and you think it should, ask the auditor's office about the parcel before you assume the bill is wrong.

sections.h2: Homestead reduction for seniors and disabled owners
sections.html:
In December 2025 the Ohio legislature doubled the tax reduction for qualified homestead owners. It first showed on first-half 2026 bills as a separate line called Local Homestead Reduction. About 11,500 of the county's 67,700 homeowners are estimated to qualify. The amount depends on local millage, and in two districts the treasurer checked it came to $354 in one township and $504 in another.

To qualify you must own and live in the home and meet one of these conditions:

  • Age 65 or older
  • Permanent and total disability
  • A veteran, or the spouse of a first responder killed in the line of duty

An Ohio adjusted income limit of $41,000 applies. Applications go through the County Auditor, whose office answers at 330-725-9754.

sections.h2: How to contest your property value
sections.html:
File a complaint with the Board of Revision, which hears appeals of auditor values. The form must reach the County Auditor's office, either postmarked or delivered, by March 31. The new postmark practice affects this deadline too, so deliver the form by hand when you can.

Call the auditor's office at 330-725-9754 for the current form before you file. The board rules on the appraised value of the property. Local taxing bodies put the levies on the ballot, and a complaint cannot change them. If you win a lower value, the bill drops with it, but the rate stays the same.

Request a current balance from the treasurer at 330-725-9748 and look up the parcel through Search and Pay Taxes. Ohio bills a year in arrears, so a sale in the first half of a year can leave the second-half installment for the prior tax year unpaid. Ask the title company how that installment will be handled at closing, and compare its figure with the bill itself.

Check the parcel's school district against the credit list above, and confirm whether a homestead reduction appears on the current bill. The treasurer's balance has to be cleared from the sale proceeds whoever the buyer is, whether a financed purchase or a cash sale. A cash buyer simply skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting steps, but the tax payoff still happens at the closing table.

Bring the latest bill, the parcel number and your closing contact to any call. Staff can then read you the exact balance, including any penalty that has been added, and tell you whether a payment is still pending.

faqs.q: What number do I call for Medina County property taxes?
faqs.a: 330-725-9748 reaches the County Treasurer. For homestead applications, call the County Auditor at 330-725-9754.

faqs.q: What were the 2026 due dates in Medina County?
faqs.a: February 27, 2026 for the first half and August 28, 2026 for the second half. A mailed payment had to be postmarked on or before those dates to avoid the 5 percent penalty.

faqs.q: How much is the late penalty?
faqs.a: It is 5 percent for payments after the due date and 10 percent once a later date passes. In 2026 that later date was March 9 for the first half and September 7 for the second half.

faqs.q: Where can I drop off a check after hours?
faqs.a: Twenty-four hour drop boxes are at the Treasurer's office in Medina, Brunswick City Hall, the Lodi Library and the Wadsworth Municipal Building. Include the bill stub.

faqs.q: Does the postmark affect the Board of Revision deadline?
faqs.a: Yes. Forms must be postmarked or physically in the auditor's office by March 31, and a postmark may not show the day you mailed. Hand delivery avoids the risk.
